Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 208 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2021) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 208 (WMU 208), Big Valley, covers an area of 1,862 km2. The WMU is located in the 
central parkland natural subregion, is primarily deeded land with limited Crown parcels, and has significant 
agricultural development in the western portion of the unit. The Red Deer River valley runs north-south bisecting 
the unit and is characterized by badlands, coniferous, and aspen forest. The valley contains Dry Island Buffalo 
Jump Provincial Park and Tolman Heritage Rangelands. There are remaining large tracts of aspen parkland on 
private lands east of the river breaks. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 208 in 2014 using 
the same strip-transect methodology, so results between 2014 and 2021 are directly comparable. See Table 1 for 
previous ungulate survey estimates for WMU 208. 
The objective of the February 2021 survey was to assess the status of ungulate populations in WMU 208 by 
determining estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of 
additional species of game management or conservation concern including carnivores, game birds,  and sensitive 
or At Risk species. 
 
Survey Method 
The transect survey was conducted flying 38 east-west lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 30% coverage (500 m wide 
survey strip, area surveyed 573 km2) from February 1-3, 2021 with a total linear survey effort of 1,145 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by species, and when possible, sex and age were recorded.  Antler 
size for deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more 
points; antlers inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). Antler drop in mule deer and 
white-tailed deer was observed with several one-antlered bucks, so buck:doe, and therefore doe:fawn ratios are 
conservative estimates. 
 
Density was  calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. Although correction factor for deer detection can be applied in parkland regions (e.g. Habib et al. 2012), 
results reported are as observed, and likely to be conservative estimates of white-tailed and mule deer abundance. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. Minimum total count of elk is reported. 
 
Results 
A total of 834 white-tailed deer were observed with an average group size of 5.0 (range 1-21)  . The estimated 
density was 1.45 deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 2,711 individuals (90% CI 2,224 – 3,199), similar to 
the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 817 white-tailed deer were classified with a buck:doe:fawn ratio of 
18:100:51. That results in an estimated 2021 winter white-tailed deer population of 298 buck, 1,604 doe, and 813 
fawn. Of the 85 white-tailed deer bucks classified, 42% were ‘small’, 51% ‘medium’, and 7% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 844 mule deer were observed with an average group size of 5.6 (range 1-20). The estimated density was 
1.47 mule deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 2,744 individuals (90% CI 2,277 – 3,211), representing a

30% decline in mule deer abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 823 mule deer were 
classified with a buck:doe:fawn ratio of 33:100:52. That results in an estimated 2021 winter mule deer population of  
494 buck, 1,481 doe, and 768 fawn. Of the 146 mule deer bucks classified, 32% were ‘small’, 47% ‘medium’, and 
20% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 181 moose were observed with an average group size of 1.7 (range 1-4). The estimated density was 
0.32 moose/km2 and the estimated abundance was 588 individuals (90% CI 451 – 726), representing a 15% 
increase in moose abundance since the last transect survey in 2014. A total of 176 moose were classified with a 
bull:cow:calf ratio of 77:100:41. That results in an estimated 2021 winter moose population of 206 bull, 270 cow, 
and 112 calf. 
 
A total of 91 elk were observed in two groups. Minimum total count of elk increased slightly from 81 in 2014. 
 
We also observed 83 coyotes, 2 sharp-tailed grouse, 2 ruffed grouse, eight great-horned owl, two golden eagle, 
and one pileated woodpecker.These are incidental observations only and should not be considered minimum total 
counts.
